editorial.headline: Forest-Products Wholesale Is Open Nationally, but Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans the wholesale trade of forestry and hunting outputs, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration there today.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the wholesale trade of products connected to forestry, forest-product collection, breeding and hunting. Its practical terrain is broad but recognisable: bamboo, sandalwood, damar resin, forestry plant seedlings, wildlife breeding and other forest outputs. It also includes the procurement and distribution of seeds and seedlings, including their sale or purchase across Indonesia’s borders. The common thread is commercial circulation: bringing these goods and inputs into trade at wholesale level.

The record makes the activity available at every listed business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That matters because the scope reaches beyond finished forest products into planting material and breeding-related outputs, areas where the object of trade can be as consequential as the trade itself. A business registering this activity should therefore read the scope as a whole, rather than reducing it to timber alone; bamboo, sandalwood, resin, forestry seedlings, wildlife breeding and other forest products are expressly within its stated reach.

Nationally, the position is clear. The activity is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In other words, the national record permits full foreign ownership for this activity. That openness is not qualified in the record by a lower national share cap, a business-scale exclusion or an additional national condition. For a founder assessing the Indonesian position in isolation, this is an activity open across the listed scales and open to foreign investment up to full ownership.

Bali is the decisive exception. A foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today. At the Large scale, OSS risk is classified as Low or Medium-Low across every stated scope, placing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registration for all Low- and Medium-Low-risk KBLI activities. The record identifies the moratorium as the reason for the block and ties that block to May 2026. National openness therefore remains real, but it does not create a PMA registration route for this activity in Bali.
